title: Why One Indian Boss in Portugal Won't Hire Portuguese
excerpt: An Indian entrepreneur's frank admission about labor costs in Lisbon is sparking debate about wages, migration, and who does Europe's hardest work.
body:
An Indian businessman based in Portugal made headlines on May 11, 2026, after publicly stating he hires only Indian workers — because Portuguese labor costs too much. His candid admission captured a tension that economists and labor advocates have quietly tracked for years.

**The Cost Gap That Drives the Choice:**
Local hiring in Portugal has become slow and expensive — a senior engineer can cost between 50,000 and 80,000 euros per year in total employer expenses. Against that backdrop, Indian workers entering under bilateral agreements represent a structurally cheaper alternative for small and mid-sized business owners navigating tight margins.

**A Corridor That Has Been Officially Open Since 2021:**
Portugal became the first EU country to sign a dedicated labor mobility pact with India. Established in 2021 and renewed through further protocols in 2025, the agreement set up a clear institutional framework for sending and receiving Indian workers. Indians are now the second-largest group of third-country nationals in Portugal, numbering 98,616 — a community built significantly on agricultural, hospitality, and service-sector labor. Indian migrant workers have become one of the nationalities that has grown the most in Portugal over the last five years, integrated into lower-skilled agricultural activities in particular.

**Why This Moment Matters Beyond One Man's Payroll:**
'The main reason Portugal has seen the number of immigrants rise is because it needs them,' says Luis Pinheiro, a former head of AIMA. But Portugal's right-wing government has simultaneously tightened immigration rules, abolishing residence permits based on declarations of interest in June 2024. The businessman's words land in a country pulled between its hunger for cheap migrant labor and political pressure to restrict new arrivals.

**What to Watch:**
Watch whether Portugal's labor ministry responds to the public controversy, and whether the 2025 renewal of the India-Portugal Bilateral Labor Agreement prompts fresh scrutiny of wage standards for Indian workers already inside the country.
